lines: A pipeline change can pass every gate your tests and your reviewers set, and it still has to run somewhere.
Here is where it runs: packaged as an image, a stack of layers, one on top of the last.
Change one line of application code, and watch how much of that stack has to be rebuilt and pushed again.
Six layers. The change lands on the instruction that copies the application's source code, fourth up from the base.
Think about what a layer actually is. Is it a record of just that one instruction, or everything up to and including it?
So how many of these six layers does the rebuild actually touch?
answer: That layer, and every layer stacked on top of it: three layers rebuild, three stay cached.
A layer is a snapshot of the whole filesystem up to that instruction, not a private diff of what the instruction itself changed.
So nothing below the change is touched, and nothing above it can survive untouched either.

lines: Watch the wave play upward from the changed layer, never downward.
The build tool's own guidance says it plainly: once a layer changes, every layer that comes after it has to run again, even when it wouldn't build anything differently.
So the practical rule is to order instructions by how often they change.
A naive build copies the dependency manifest and the source code together, so any source edit forces every dependency to reinstall.
Reorder it: copy the manifest first, install, and copy the source last. The same edit now rebuilds two layers instead of four.
Now delete a file in a later instruction. Does the image get smaller?
It can't. The layers underneath are read only, so nothing can be removed from them.
What actually happens is a tiny marker file gets added on top, telling the runtime to hide that name. The bytes underneath never leave the image.
A build stage can carry a whole compiler toolchain and its cache. None of that has to ship.
Copy only the finished program into a second, fresh, minimal base, and the build stage's layers fall away entirely.
The project that publishes these minimal bases states its smallest image at about two mebibytes, against a lightweight distribution's five and a full distribution's one hundred and twenty four.
A container's own writable layer dies the moment the container does.
A named volume or a bind mount lives on past it, and a shared network lets services find each other by name instead of a changing address.
Bring up a database, an object store and a message broker together, and one plain ordering rule only decides which starts first, not which is actually ready.
Pair that ordering with a condition that waits for each service's own health check, and the application never greets a database that hasn't finished starting up.
Last choice: environment variable, or a mounted file?
An environment variable is simple, but anyone who can inspect the running container can read it in plain text.
A mounted file keeps a secret out of that inspection surface, readable only from inside the container's own filesystem.
An image is a frozen filesystem. Running it is something else entirely: a process on a machine, kept inside a boundary the kernel enforces with a number written to one of its own files.
What that boundary does when the process asks for more than it was given is exactly where we go next.
